tweets.text:
This is *not* how you use AI in trading. People actually doing this will get rekt.

AI has made backtesting fast and accessible to anyone with data. What it has not removed is your need to judge the output and catch the mistakes made along the way. And that's the trap, because not all friction is the same. Using AI well is mostly one skill: telling apart friction that only costs you time from friction that is actively training you. The key question is which friction you need to keep and go through yourself to be able to judge the output. This way you learn about lookahead bias, overfitting, etc. That's the intellectual debt you accumulate when you let AI handle the whole process.

People who outsource all of it make AI torture historical data until it confesses to anything. I've literally watched people backtest a strategy, find that it underperforms on certain days of the week, and simply delete those periods from the sample. To them, it looked like refinement, but it's quite the *opposite*.

Which is exactly what Step 4 tells you to do. "Analyse this trade history and tell me how to improve this strategy" is an instruction to overfit. There's very little fitting the average person can do before fucking things up big time. In practice, AI is just amplifying the same old biases with a lot more computational power and speed. You just make them at scale and get rekt quicker.

That being said, backtests are in themselves very tricky, mainly due to path dependence, which means your results aren't just about whether your strategy works.

What I want as a trader is the ability to find out I'm wrong. To progress in trading (or any intellectual domain), you must formulate your beliefs in a way that makes them explicitly falsifiable. By intentionally making your ideas vulnerable to being disproven, you eliminate ambiguity and create a pathway to objective "truth".

What's quite often missing in discretionary is the scientific rigor that profitability demands. A sound approach starts with an idea, a hypothesis about how or why price behaves the way it does. From there, you ask "how could I prove this wrong?" and then do exactly that, as ruthlessly as possible. Most of your ideas will turn out to be dogshit. That's fine. That's just the way it is. Trading is a discipline of structured skepticism.

Whenever someone shows you the total altcoin market cap, you should have in mind what the equal-weight version looks like. The *aggregate* alt market can look alive and well while the *average* alt holder is still getting cooked brutally. Maybe you know that feeling, right?

"The altcoin market" is a statistical artifact, not something anyone owns. Aggregate alt market cap is a cap-weighted number, so broadly speaking, it reflects whatever handful of big coins are pumping the hardest.

Total alt cap is up roughly 12x since 2019 while an equal-weight basket of the top 200 is below its starting value (data through July, too lazy to update the chart rn). That gap is the whole danger of talking about alts in general.

Holding some handpicked coins you're convinced are the future is *not* exposure to that chart. Alt cap is being carried by whatever is big and hot right now, which is almost certainly not the thing you're still averaging down on for fundamental reasons. You're taking a bet that your specific picks are among the few doing the carrying (which is a bad bet because chances are you're wrong; ask me how I know).

If you want exposure to trending altcoins, the right object of analysis is trend itself.

Tops and bottoms are arbitrary reference points with little relevance to sound strategies. Most money is made in between. You don’t have to care about them at all. You shouldn’t.

You can be wrong about the low and still make money, or nail it and still lose by sizing badly, exiting early, etc. There’s so much levels to this. The best trade of your year will likely have a mediocre entry and the best call of your year might be one you never sized into.

It’s a separate game with a separate, public scoreboard. So people naturally drift toward the one that gives feedback without noticing they switched games.

For the most part, the word "lagging" is doing dishonest work. People use it to reframe underperformance as opportunity, as if there's a queue and your bag is waiting for its turn. In most cases there is no lag, there's just weakness. No demand, no reason for anyone to buy this shit.

"Lagging" implies a relationship: This shitter belongs with the leaders and is temporarily behind. But that relationship is something you asserted. Strip it away and you're left with the plain observation that nobody's bidding this shit.

In a market driven by trend and momentum, you specifically want the *opposite*. You want exposure to what's already strong, already moving, because that's where capital is actually flowing. It's way better to buy into what is already strong than to assume what will become strong in the future.

tweets.text:
AI models are trained on whatever exists about trading and the truth is that most of that material is dogshit. Most of it was never even tested and the strategies that were tested usually turn out to be dogshit once you test them. So the worst thing you can do is open up an AI and ask it directly for trading advice, have it code a bot or some other dogshit because it just hands you back a polished version of the same dogshit.

The better path is to figure out for yourself what actually works, through your own testing, before you bring AI into the picture at all. Once you've built that foundation, turn it into a structured knowledge base of vetted, working ideas. Then you have the AI sift through that knowledge base and it becomes genuinely useful, because now it's reasoning from the right sources instead of regurgitating the dogshit.

tweets.text:
The whole plumbing meme is quite funny because it's one of the best analogies for what you should be doing in markets.

The plumber gets paid precisely because the job is the one nobody wants to touch. He is useful to the system he operates in and he could tell you in one sentence what he's being paid for. So the question to run in markets is the plumber's question: what problem am I solving here and is it unpleasant enough that most people are quietly avoiding it?

Most people in trading can't answer that question. They stare at charts, name patterns and build frameworks around things that nobody is compensating them for. There is no problem being solved and no one on the other side who needed it done. They're doing work, but they're not doing anyone's plumbing.

We all should strive to be like plumbers.
